fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Why Tolkien Called Fairies Natural", "body": "Chance reads from Tolkien's essay On Fairy Stories, where man rather than the fairy is called supernatural, and Becca Tarnas hears a not-so-hidden ecological ethic in it: humans imagine themselves separate from nature, while elves are of the natural world. She points to Iceland, where by her account about 5% of people firmly believe in the hidden folk, 5% firmly deny them and the rest leave room, so roads curve around rocks said to be elf homes. She traces a path from myth to legend to fairy story to fantasy novel, and argues that the imagination itself is a natural feature of the cosmos."}, {"title": "Language as a Kind of Spell", "body": "Chance reads Tolkien's rebuttal of Max Müller's view of mythology as a disease of language, and his praise of the adjective as the most potent spell in faerie. Becca explains that Tolkien was a philologist, a lover of the word, who saw words as carrying their meaning rather than as arbitrary labels, and she links spell to spelling and grammar to glamour. Drawing on Owen Barfield's Poetic Diction and Saving the Appearances, she describes how the Latin spiritus once meant spirit, wind and breath at once. Chance asks whether splitting those meanings made it easier to treat the earth as lifeless."}, {"title": "Childlike Wonder and the Inner Child", "body": "Chance brings up Tolkien's line that whoever would enter the kingdom of fairy should have the heart of a little child, and asks what is happening to the inner child in the collective psyche. Becca separates childlike from childish, borrowing the beginner's mind of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, and argues that many adults have lost their wonder without ever being initiated into adulthood. For her, a true adult protects that inner child as an everyday practice. Chance names the failure adultism and offers the adept as its opposite, pointing to Gandalf, Aragorn, and Frodo, who saves the Shire but not for himself."}, {"title": "Gandalf, Saruman and the Limits of Reason", "body": "Becca contrasts Gandalf with Saruman, head of the White Council, who would never sit down with hobbits over ale and pipe weed. She ties humility to humus, the soil, and to being human, and sees that closeness to the earth as the reason Gandalf alone among the Istari succeeds, while Saruman eyes the Shire as country to industrialize and sell off. Chance argues that Saruman's slide began with fear dressed up as logic: once you use evil as a means to good ends, evil has already won. Becca adds that reason matters but needs balancing with imagination, emotion and embodiment, citing Gregory Bateson."}, {"title": "Recovery, Escape and Re-Enchantment", "body": "Becca takes up Tolkien's defense of fantasy against the charge of escapism: the escape of the prisoner is not the flight of the deserter, and the world beyond the prison walls is still real. In his essay, she notes, the land of fairy is our world, holding sun, moon, sea and mortal humans when they are enchanted, and she says Tolkien is clear that Middle-earth is our earth. She frames recovery as reclaiming a birthright of enchantment while keeping what the modern split has won, such as individual rights, and sees the early pandemic as a pivotal moment. Chance worries fear could revive old divisions like xenophobia."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Becca Tarnas returns to talk about the esoteric wisdom in JRR Tolkien's works. These "Fairy Stories" aren't your Mother Goose nursery rhymes; in the Perilous Realm, you'll find mystical enchantment and mortal endangerment in equal measure. Tune in to hear about legends of the hidden folk, the mythic consciousness of our ancestors, and how the love of language, magic of words, and the archetype of the inner child can help you recover the beauty and wonder of life.
